name: HTML & CSS
description: Semantics, the box model, flexbox and grid, specificity, stacking contexts and accessible markup.

modules.name: Semantic HTML & Accessibility
modules.description: Markup that means something — to browsers, to search engines and to assistive technology.

cards.prompt: Why prefer `<button>`, `<nav>`, `<main>` and `<article>` over styled `<div>`s?
cards.answer: Semantic elements bring built-in behaviour and meaning: keyboard focus and activation, correct roles in the accessibility tree, landmark navigation for screen readers, and better parsing by search engines and reader modes.
cards.explanation: A `<div onclick>` is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users unless you re-implement `tabindex`, Enter/Space handling, `role` and focus styling — four chances to get it wrong. The native element gets all of that free and correct.

cards.prompt: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA — use a ___ HTML element instead if one exists.
cards.answer: native
cards.explanation: ARIA changes only how assistive tech reports an element; it adds no behaviour. `role="button"` on a div still needs manual keyboard handling. Bad ARIA is worse than none because it lies to the accessibility tree.

resources.title: W3C — Using ARIA: rules of ARIA use

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this form field?
cards.answer: No `<label for>` association, and placeholder is not a label — it vanishes on input and often fails contrast. Use `<label for="email">Email</label><input id="email" type="email">`.
cards.explanation: A proper label is announced by screen readers, and clicking it focuses the field — a real usability win on touch. `type="email"` also brings the right mobile keyboard and free validation.

cards.prompt: What are the headline WCAG 2.2 AA requirements developers hit most often?
cards.answer: Contrast of 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 for large text and UI components), every function reachable by keyboard with a visible focus indicator, text resizable to 200%, correct heading order, alt text for meaningful images, and errors identified in text rather than by colour alone.
cards.explanation: Most of these are testable automatically (axe, Lighthouse) but automation catches perhaps a third of real issues. Tab through the page and use a screen reader once per feature — it finds what scanners cannot.

modules.name: Layout & the Cascade
modules.description: Specificity, box model, flexbox, grid and stacking — the parts that cause the most confusion.

cards.prompt: How is CSS specificity calculated, and what beats it?
cards.answer: As a tuple (inline, ID, class/attribute/pseudo-class, element/pseudo-element), compared left to right. Later rules win ties. `!important` overrides normal declarations, and inline styles beat selectors — but layer order and `!important` in earlier cascade layers can still take precedence.
cards.explanation: The practical lesson is to keep specificity flat: one class per component, no ID selectors in stylesheets, no `!important` arms races. Cascade layers (`@layer`) let you order framework and app styles explicitly instead of by accident.

cards.prompt: How wide is this element rendered, with and without `box-sizing: border-box`?
cards.answer: 244px by default (content-box: 200 + 40 padding + 4 border); exactly 200px with `border-box`.
cards.explanation: `content-box` is the CSS default and almost never what you want, which is why virtually every reset sets `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box }`. With border-box, `width` means the visible width.

cards.prompt: Flexbox vs Grid
cards.answer: Flexbox lays out along one axis and sizes from content; Grid defines two-dimensional rows and columns from the container.

left.title: Flexbox
points: One dimension: a row or a column
Ideal for toolbars, button groups, cards in a row

right.title: Grid
points: Layout-in sizing: you define the tracks
Ideal for page layout and complex forms

cards.explanation: They compose — a grid page layout with flex components inside is the normal pattern. `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` gives a responsive card grid with no media queries at all.

cards.prompt: Your modal has `z-index: 9999` and still renders behind a sidebar. Why?
cards.answer: An ancestor created a stacking context — via `transform`, `opacity < 1`, `filter`, `will-change`, `position` with a z-index, `isolation`, or `contain`. Inside it, z-index is only compared against siblings in that context.
cards.explanation: z-index is not global. Once an ancestor forms a stacking context, no descendant can escape above the ancestor's own level. Fixes: portal the modal to `<body>`, remove the offending property, or use the top-layer `<dialog>` element which sidesteps stacking entirely.

cards.prompt: An animation stutters. Which properties should you animate, and why?
cards.answer: `transform` and `opacity`. They can be handled by the compositor without triggering layout or paint; animating `width`, `top`, `margin` or `box-shadow` forces reflow and repaint every frame.
cards.explanation: The pipeline is style → layout → paint → composite. Layout is the expensive stage, and it invalidates everything after it. Reading a layout property (`offsetHeight`) right after a write forces synchronous layout — the 'layout thrashing' pattern to batch away.

cards.prompt: What do custom properties, `clamp()`, container queries and `:has()` each solve?
cards.answer: Custom properties give runtime-themable values inherited through the tree; `clamp(min, preferred, max)` gives fluid sizing without breakpoints; container queries style by the parent's size rather than the viewport; `:has()` is the long-awaited parent selector.
cards.explanation: Together they remove most of what preprocessors and JavaScript were doing. A component sized with container queries works correctly in a sidebar and in a full-width hero without knowing where it was placed.

cards.prompt: What do these selectors match: `.card p`, `.card > p`, `h2 + p`, `a:hover`, `li:nth-child(2n)`, `p::first-line` and `input[type="email"]`?
cards.answer: Descendant (`.card p`: any p inside .card), child (`.card > p`: direct children only), adjacent sibling (`h2 + p`: the p immediately after an h2), pseudo-class (`a:hover`: a state), structural pseudo-class (`li:nth-child(2n)`: even items), pseudo-element (`p::first-line`: part of an element), and attribute selector (`input[type="email"]`).
cards.explanation: Pseudo-classes select elements in a state; pseudo-elements style a part of an element or generated content (`::before`). Modern additions — `:is()`, `:where()` (zero specificity), `:has()` and `:focus-visible` — replace much of what used to require extra classes or JavaScript.

modules.name: Layout, Units & Responsive Design
modules.description: The box model in flow, display and positioning, units, centring, responsive techniques and motion.

cards.prompt: Block vs inline vs inline-block
cards.answer: Block elements start on a new line and take the full available width, honouring width, height and vertical margins. Inline elements flow within text, ignore width and height, and vertical margins do not push lines apart. Inline-block flows inline but is sized like a block.

right.title: inline / inline-block
points: inline: flows in text, ignores width/height
inline: vertical margins do not affect layout
inline-block: in the text flow but sizable

cards.explanation: Knowing an element's display type explains most "why won't this margin/width apply" questions — a `<span>` or `<a>` ignores `width` until it becomes inline-block, block, or a flex item. Flex and grid containers change how their children are laid out entirely.

cards.prompt: What do `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed` and `sticky` positioning do?
cards.answer: `relative` offsets an element from its normal spot and makes it the containing block for absolute children. `absolute` removes it from flow, positioned against the nearest positioned ancestor. `fixed` positions against the viewport. `sticky` scrolls normally until a threshold, then sticks within its container.
cards.explanation: The classic surprise: an `absolute` child positions against the page because no ancestor is positioned — add `position: relative` to the intended parent. `sticky` silently fails when an ancestor has `overflow: hidden`. A `transform` on an ancestor turns `fixed` into positioning relative to that ancestor.

cards.prompt: When should you use `rem`, `em`, `%`, `px`, `vw`/`vh` and `ch`?
cards.answer: `rem` (relative to the root font size) for font sizes and spacing so everything scales with the user's font setting; `em` for things that should scale with the local font size; `%` relative to the parent; `px` for hairlines and borders; `vw`/`vh`/`dvh` for viewport-relative sizing; `ch` for readable line lengths (`max-width: 65ch`).
cards.explanation: Font sizes in `px` ignore the user's browser font preference — an accessibility failure. `100vh` on mobile includes space behind browser UI; use `100dvh`. `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem)` combines them into fluid, bounded type.

cards.prompt: The gap between the two paragraphs is 24px, not 40px. Why?
cards.answer: Vertical margins between adjacent blocks collapse: the larger of the two wins instead of adding up. It also happens between a parent and its first or last child when nothing (border, padding, or a new formatting context) separates them.
cards.explanation: Margin collapsing never happens in flex or grid layouts, which is one reason layouts built with `gap` are more predictable. Consistently using margin in one direction only (for example, only `margin-block-start`) sidesteps most surprises.

cards.prompt: What is the simplest way to centre an element horizontally and vertically?
cards.answer: Make the parent a grid or flex container: `display: grid; place-items: center;` or `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;`. For horizontal centring of a block with a width, `margin-inline: auto` also works.
cards.explanation: Older tricks — absolute positioning with `translate(-50%, -50%)`, table cells, line-height hacks — are rarely needed now. Remember the container needs a height for vertical centring to be visible.

cards.prompt: What are the essentials of responsive design?
cards.answer: The viewport meta tag (`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`), fluid layouts with flex and grid, mobile-first media queries (`min-width` breakpoints chosen where the content breaks, not by device), responsive images, and fluid type with `clamp()`.
cards.explanation: Without the viewport tag, mobile browsers render a desktop-width page and zoom out. Container queries let components adapt to their own space, and `prefers-color-scheme`/`prefers-reduced-motion` adapt to user settings as well as screen size.

cards.prompt: Your site has parallax scrolling and large animated transitions. What must you add for accessibility?
cards.answer: Respect `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`: remove or tone down large motion, parallax and auto-playing animation for users who have asked their OS for less motion. Also provide pause controls for anything that moves for more than five seconds.
cards.explanation: Large motion can trigger vestibular disorders — dizziness and nausea — so this is a WCAG requirement, not a nicety. Subtle opacity fades are usually fine; zooms, spins and parallax are not.

cards.prompt: Utility-first CSS (Tailwind) vs component-scoped CSS (CSS Modules, BEM)
cards.answer: Utility-first composes small single-purpose classes in the markup; scoped approaches write semantic class names per component with styles kept in separate files or modules.

left.title: Utility-first
points: No naming, no dead CSS, tiny output
Long class lists; needs components to avoid repetition

right.title: Scoped / BEM
points: Scoping prevents leaks (Modules) or convention does (BEM)
Naming effort; unused CSS can linger

cards.explanation: Both solve the same underlying problem: global CSS where any rule can affect anything. Pick one approach per codebase, back it with design tokens (custom properties for colour, spacing, type), and let the build remove unused CSS.

modules.name: Accessibility & HTML in Depth
modules.description: Headings and landmarks, keyboard focus, live regions, dialogs, forms and images.

cards.prompt: Why do heading levels and landmarks matter to screen-reader users?
cards.answer: Screen-reader users navigate by headings and landmarks the way sighted users skim: jumping heading to heading, or straight to `<main>`, `<nav>` or `<footer>`. One `<h1>` per page and heading levels without skips turn the page into a navigable outline.
cards.explanation: Choose heading levels for structure, never for font size — restyle with CSS instead. A "skip to main content" link as the first focusable element lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation.

cards.prompt: What accessibility bugs are in this code?
cards.answer: `outline: none` removes the visible focus indicator, so keyboard users cannot see where they are, and a positive `tabindex` hijacks the natural tab order. Style focus with `:focus-visible` instead of removing it, and use only `tabindex="0"` (focusable in order) or `-1` (focusable by script).
cards.explanation: Every interactive element must be reachable and operable by keyboard alone, in a logical order that matches the visual one. When content opens or closes — modals, menus, route changes in SPAs — move focus deliberately and return it afterwards.

cards.prompt: How do you announce dynamic updates, such as "Item added to cart", to screen-reader users?
cards.answer: Put the message in an ARIA live region: an element present from page load with `aria-live="polite"` (announced when the user is idle) or `role="status"`; use `role="alert"` (assertive) only for urgent errors. Changing its text triggers the announcement.
cards.explanation: Content that appears silently elsewhere on the page is invisible to someone who cannot see it. Inserting the live region at the same moment as the message often fails — create it early and update its contents.

cards.prompt: Why use the native `<dialog>` element for modals?
cards.answer: `dialog.showModal()` renders it in the top layer (above everything, no z-index fights), makes the rest of the page inert, traps focus inside, closes on Escape, and restores focus to the opener when closed. Styling the backdrop uses `::backdrop`.
cards.explanation: Hand-built modal divs routinely miss focus trapping, Escape handling, inert background and focus restoration — each an accessibility failure. `<dialog>` gets them right by default, as does the `popover` attribute for non-modal overlays.

cards.prompt: What does native HTML give you for forms, and what must you still do?
cards.answer: Input types (`email`, `tel`, `number`, `date`, `url`) with suitable mobile keyboards, constraint attributes (`required`, `min`, `max`, `pattern`, `maxlength`), `autocomplete` tokens for autofill and password managers, and `<fieldset>`/`<legend>` for grouping.
cards.explanation: You must still validate on the server — client validation is only UX. Connect error messages to fields with `aria-describedby`, describe errors in text rather than colour alone, and never block pasting into password fields.

cards.prompt: How do you write `alt` text for a product photo, a decorative divider, and an icon-only "delete" button?
cards.answer: Product photo: describe what matters in context ("Red leather satchel with brass buckle"). Decorative divider: `alt=""` so it is skipped. Icon-only button: give the *button* an accessible name (`aria-label="Delete"` or visually hidden text) and hide the icon itself from assistive technology.
cards.explanation: Alt text conveys the image's purpose, not its pixels, and should not start with "image of". Omitting `alt` entirely is worse than empty, because screen readers then read the filename.
